history.p: The text of the present cantata is by one of Scheibe’s close acquaintances, the writer Johann Elias Schlegel who arrived in Copenhagen a couple of years after Scheibe. Scheibe received the text in 1746, and a year later the cantata for orchestra and vocal soloists was finished and performed both in Copenhagen as well as other places. In connection with the publication of Tragische Kantaten during 1763–64, Scheibe reworked and revised 'Prokris und Cephalus' for a harpsichord instead of orchestra. In his introduction to the new version which appeared in 1765, Scheibe explains the revision of the work in more detail. The cantata is mentioned in a review of the publication in Bibliothek der schönen Wissenschaften (1765) edited by Christian Felix Weiße: 'Procris and Cephalus also have their great beauty, and how could they avoid having it when one thinks of the author: it is in fact an imitation of Rousseau ‒ but the imitation is by a man who was himself a poet. Regarding the musical execution we cannot say more than it is entirely worthy of the author, and one is led to wonder whether it is the composer or the author who has most happily managed to express the passions. Mr. S. promises perhaps a second part, and thereby encourages the Muses to unite so that he may fulfil a praiseworthy vow.' A year after Scheibe passed away, the cantata was reprinted by Hellmann in Altona.

annot.p: 'Prokris und Cephalus hat auch seine großen Schönheiten, und wie sollten sie es nicht haben, wenn man an dem Verfasser denkt: sie ist eigentlich eine Nachahmung des Rousseau, aber die Nachahmung eines Mannes, der selbst ein Dichter war. Von der musikalischen Ausführung können wir nichts mehr sagen, als daß sie des Verfassers vollkommen würdig ist, und man oft in Ungewißheit geräht, welcher von beyden, der Componist oder der Dichter, den Ausdruck der Leidenschaften am glücklichsten getroffen habe. Hr. S. verspricht vielleicht einen zweyten Theil, und muntert dadurch die Musen auf, sich zu vereinigen, damit er ein löbliches Versprechen erfüllen möge.'

physDesc.watermark: a visible emblem consisting of the royal monogram: two crowned and interwoven Cs and 6s (one pair in mirror image) of King Christian VI (reigned: 1730–46; cf. Voorn:IV.5); and the countermark 'I D' (Johann Drewsen).
physDesc.physMedium: In 2o; upright format, consisting of 2, 2, 2, and 2 nested bifolios; music (fols. 1r–16v; foliated 1–16 in ink (Scheibe)); in all 16 folios. Hand-ruled paper, between 20 and 22 staves (7 mm; single rastrum used) in light brown ink and music in black ink; on many pages the bottom staves have not been used. Scheibe’s ink autograph working copy contains numerous changes in ink as well some in pencil (continuo figures in the fondamento e.g.); crosses at various bar lines suggest that a transcription was made. Bottom stave on fol. 16v contains a non-autograph eight-bar music incipit in G major in a script suggesting a professional copyist. The same hand is also found in one of Scheibe's organ works (SchW A4:001).
Full cardboard binding of the nineteenth century and ex libris ‘Ex | bibliotheca | Poelchaviana’ on upper paste-down; thin paper of a rather inferior quality.

physDesc.watermark: partly visible watermarks on flyleaves, of which the front one consists of 'J. Bassuet' with grapes above, dating from the end of the eighteenth century or the beginning of the nineteenth century; the end flyleaf has 'M DANG MOIS', where 'mois' is similar to Gravell:5722.
physDesc.physMedium: In 8o; marbled endpaper, front flyleaf, title page (sig. [*1r]), blank page (sig. [*1v]), foreword (sigs. *2r–*3v), table of contents (sig. *4r–v), text (pp. 3–320), end flyleaf, marbled endpaper. The relevant pages concerning the present cantata are pp. 210–13. According to Schlegel's brother and editor, the text which Scheibe employed for his published cantata (1765) agrees with his father's manuscript (cf. introduction to Schlegels Werke (1766), vol. 4, pp. 205–06).
Full-bound in a contemporary leather binding, partly ornamented and with title and the royal monogram of Christian VII (reigned 1766–1808) on spine. Paper of a good quality.
